title: Pliny the Elder Sails Toward Vesuvius
text:
In August 79 AD, Pliny the Elder, the great naturalist and author of the Natural History, commanded the Roman fleet at Misenum, on the Bay of Naples. His widowed sister and her son, the seventeen-year-old Pliny the Younger, were staying with him. Years later the nephew described what happened in two letters to the historian Tacitus.

Early one afternoon his mother pointed out a huge cloud rising over the bay, shaped like an umbrella pine. The scholar in Pliny the Elder wanted to see it more closely, and he ordered a boat. He invited his nephew along, but the young man replied that he would rather keep studying. Then a message came from a woman whose villa lay at the foot of Vesuvius, begging for rescue. Pliny turned his scientific trip into a rescue mission, launched warships, and steered straight toward the danger while others fled.

Unable to land, he went on to Stabiae, where he calmed his frightened friend Pomponianus by bathing, dining cheerfully and going to sleep. In the night, as ash piled up, they fled to the shore with pillows tied to their heads. There Pliny collapsed and died.

At Misenum, the nephew lived through his own night of terror. As they fled, his mother begged him to leave her behind, since she was old and slow and he could escape alone. He refused, took her hand and made her walk faster. Both survived.
lesson: Courage and duty can be passed from one generation to the next by example. In a crisis, the people we refuse to leave behind define who we are.
people: Pliny the Elder, Pliny the Younger, his mother Plinia, Pomponianus
location: Misenum and Stabiae, Bay of Naples, Italy
caveat: The traditional date of 24 August has been questioned, and some scholars place the eruption in the autumn.
